doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

chapter: Discovering jazz and the trad band
title: Records, Kid Ory and the Apex Stompers
summary: He wanted to play traditional jazz like Kid Ory, bought 78s, and the band played for beer until its London billing coincided with his call-up.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: bowled over by this. Strictly traditional jazz. I wanted to play traditional jazz. By that time I knew who Kid Ory was and I was aware that that was the kind of jazz music I wanted to have a go at. And we all felt the same, you know, quite purist and just wanted to have a go at it.
Were those records fairly easy to get?

Oh yeah, yeah. Not in great quantity, I mean it was the days of 78s. I mean you kind of went down to the record shop to see what had come in, what had been released. And the first record I bought, I can still remember, was a 78 of Jelly Roll Morton “Smokehouse Blues,” the second one was Kid Ory’s “Oh Didn’t He Ramble,” and that’s the band sound that we thought ahh, that’s what we want to do. We want to play like Kid Ory’s Creole Jazz Band. I’m not quite sure we made that, but that’s what we wanted to do.
Did you ever make any money doing it?

We played youth clubs and school things. So what you might get was beer and sandwiches. I don’t think anyone ever paid us actual money, but they kind of said come along and play and you can have as much beer to drink or you can have as much food as you want, or something like that. And the irony of it was that we’d got just about our real professional breakthrough, if that was going to be it, when we were named as the interval band at a dance in the center of London, where there was a quite well known jazz band as the principal band. And the tickets were printed, our band was called the Apex Stompers. And there was Dave Carey’s Jazz Band, which was quite well known, and the Apex Stompers. And that was week I was called up to go to military service. So that was our kind of prime moment, and I wasn’t there. So there you are you see. It was a tough break. I had to go to the Army. I couldn’t sort of say to the Army look I’ve got this important opportunity.
